title: Example: rate limiting for the orders API

slides.title: Rate limiting for the orders API
slides.subtitle: Clients that flood the API now get a clear 429 instead of slowing everyone down
slides.narration: This pull request adds rate limiting to the orders API. A client that sends too many requests now gets a clear too many requests answer, instead of slowing the service down for everybody else.

slides.title: What changes for users
bullets: Each API key gets **100 requests per minute**

bullets.text: Over the limit: `429 Too Many Requests`
sub: `Retry-After` header says when to come back

bullets: Limits are shared across all API replicas
slides.narration: From the outside, three things change. Every API key gets a budget of one hundred requests per minute. When a client goes over, it receives a four twenty nine with a retry after header. And the budget is shared across all replicas, so adding replicas does not multiply the limit.

slides.title: Where the change lands

components.name: Orders API
components.change: New rate limit middleware in the request chain

components.name: Redis
components.change: Holds one counter per API key and window

slides.narration: The system has four components. The gateway and the database are untouched. The orders API gets a new middleware, and a new component appears: a reddiss instance that holds the counters.

slides.title: A new dependency: shared counters
slides.caption: Every request now makes one extra round trip to Redis before reaching the handler
slides.narration: Architecturally, this is the one thing to remember. The orders API gains a dependency on reddiss. Every request makes one extra round trip to increment a counter before the handler runs.

slides.title: The middleware fails open
slides.note: **Why it matters:** an outage of the new dependency degrades protection, not availability.
slides.narration: The most important design decision is in the middleware. If reddiss is unreachable, the limiter lets traffic through and counts the event in a metric. So losing the new dependency costs you protection, but never availability.

slides.title: Trying it on a live environment
slides.narration: Let's try it on a running environment.

slides.title: Send 105 requests with one key
slides.command: for i in $(seq 105); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' $API/orders; done | sort | uniq -c
slides.narration: First, I send one hundred and five requests with the same key. One hundred succeed, and the last five are rejected.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.narration: To recap. A per key limit shared across replicas, one new dependency that fails open, and a thirty second way to see it working. Thanks for watching.
